author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
A non-AI naive engineer questions me the danger of being overly dependent on using AI doing my daily work.  What would you do if AI is offline? 

My response to him is what would you do if there is a power outage in the office.  Do you write code with pen and paper?   

If GPT or Claude is offline, then it is like a power outage, we go home early and enjoy nature.

author.name: Lars Faye
author.headline: B2B Full Stack // Technical Director // Coding Mentor

comments.text: Wow, that a demented take. A truly sad period for the industry.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text: Lars Faye You will get used to it. They said the same thing about the compiler back then too

author.name: Lars Faye
author.headline: B2B Full Stack // Technical Director // Coding Mentor

replies.text:
Horace Chan The compiler didn't atrophy the cognitive skills of the programming discipline. And you could still code if your compiler wasn't working for whatever reason. In fact, you could write your own if that situation arose. Apparently, without an LLM, you're somehow completely stupefied and useless.

"We see a future where intelligence is a utility like electricity or water and people buy it from us on a meter and use it for whatever they want to use it for" - Sam Altman

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Lars Faye seriously?  Do you know how to write assembly?  Trust me, you DON'T want to write assembly by hand if you can avoid it.  That's my day job many years ago.

If the compiler is offline, it is still faster to wait for it to come back online then write the code in assembly.

And who said you can't train your own LLM model just like writing your own compiler?

author.name: Lars Faye
author.headline: B2B Full Stack // Technical Director // Coding Mentor

replies.text:
Horace Chan The skills one can derive from writing assembly can still apply to modern day programming. The skills one derives from prompting an LLM...don't translate to anything whatsoever. It's not just me saying this: the studies are out there.

https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2422633122
https://dl.acm.org/doi/epdf/10.1145/3632620.3671116

Anyway...you keep doing you. It would just be nice if you stop giving such shortsighted advice to others.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Lars Faye You don't prompt LLM.  If you only prompts, you are doing it wrong.

Input -> process -> output

If you don't like the output, fix the input.  Same for all computing, same for LLM.  LLM is just computing.

Using LLM effectively is more like crafting SQL and the DB schema than talking to another human. There is no intelligence in AI.  It is just how you organize information

author.name: Lars Faye
author.headline: B2B Full Stack // Technical Director // Coding Mentor

replies.text:
Horace Chan Now you're just playing with semantics and phrasing to obfuscate the underlying message. I'm fully educated and experienced on how to work with these autoregressive statistical machine learning next token predictors. And I've written extensively about them.

https://larsfaye.com/articles/agentic-coding-is-a-trap
https://cheewebdevelopment.com/dont-vibe-code-delegate-responsible-development-with-llms/

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Lars Faye I guess it depends on your view on what is LLM.

To me, LLM is more like a database and search engine than AI.  If the solution exists within its weights and context, and you have a deterministic way to check pass/fail, then eventually LLM will be convergent to the solution.

The key is how to express any problem in this format, so it fits the operating parameters of an LLM.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Lars Faye code is no longer relevant and it never should be in the first place

Data structure, algorithm, network latency, distributed work load, those still matter with AI

AI liberates us from stupid language wars and framework wars, so we can once again focus on the real thing that matters

author.headline: B2B Full Stack // Technical Director // Coding Mentor

replies.text:
Horace Chan Mmhm. And the irony of it all: none of those skills are of any use if you don't go through the friction to understand how those elements work, on a tangible and visceral level. The very friction that you're advocating we skip over, apparently, by just taking the day off when the friction-alleviating-machine isn't online. Fascinating.

I suppose we'll just grow our future senior engineers in a greenhouse somewhere!

But for old folks like us, we already learned most of it the hard way, now we can just speed run anything using AI

author.name: Gleb Rezoun
author.headline: Senior Backend Engineer | Node.js & Go | High-Load Distributed Systems

comments.text:
I don't buy the power-outage analogy. We should not normalize over-dependence on AI.

I'd be seriously concerned if an engineer on my team could not work without it. AI should make you faster, but you should still be able to read code, debug an issue, and make a change when the tool is unavailable.

Otherwise, it is not an accelerator. It is a dependency.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Gleb Rezoun only a few unlucky souls have to learn how to read code, debug an issue at code level.  Most people should operate at the abstraction one level above.

How do I know?  I am an unlucky soul knows how to debug firmware reading assembly code in the compiler era.   Most of my software team are happily working at the C/C++ abstraction layer.

author.name: Namir Sagheenanajar
author.headline: President at Initech Solutions

comments.text:
Interesting analogy, but it also highlights a bit of irony.

"We'll just go home and enjoy nature" sounds great... until we remember that the AI ecosystem increasingly depends on massive data centers consuming enormous amounts of electricity, water, land, and infrastructure while employing relatively few people compared to the industries they're attempting to displace.

Perhaps a better long-term strategy is not becoming so dependent on any single external service that an outage means productivity simply stops. Resilience has always been a hallmark of good engineering.

There's a difference between using AI as a powerful tool and designing an entire profession around the assumption that someone else's infrastructure will always be available, affordable, and acting in your best interests.

Namir Sagheenanajar nay... expensive humans who buy designer clothes, fancy cars and flying business class everywhere waste way more energy than data centers.

Replacing all the BS jobs with AI and the world can save a lot of energy.  AI is very good at BS.
